The directness of a free kick relates to the severity of the infringement - direct free kicks are awarded for more severe issues and may score a goal without touching any other player, while indirect free kicks are for less severe issues and must touch another player before counting as a goal. It's fairly reasonable that the team being awarded the free kick would never have the extra burden of the free kick being considered direct against their own goal - the kick being direct serves to punish the defending team, and shouldn't put the offense at any risk at all. An indirect free kick certainly wouldn't count if kicked directly into either goal, and it would be odd if the offense was put at risk of an own-goal by their opponent committing a greater direct-kick infraction, when they wouldn't have been at any risk at all had the opponent committed a lesser indirect-kick infraction.

Effectively, a free kick is always considered indirect against your own goal. Other types of play restarts are similar - a throw-in is always indirect and cannot score without being touched by another player, whether it's in your own goal or not.

Yes, there exist official specifications for badminton rackets. The BWF Laws of Badminton limit a racket to 680 mm in length and 230 mm in width. The stringed area has its own limits, maximum overall length 280 mm, maximum overall width 220 mm, subject to permissible throat extension. Interestingly, BWF rules do not stipulate a maximum or minimum weight for rackets. So different rackets can have different weights by law. The “U” weight categories often printed on rackets are mostly manufacturer conventions and not a universal BWF specification.

There are various attempts to develop such metrics; while nothing is standardized (as far as I know), the activity tracking app Strava has a feature called Grade Adjusted Pace:

Grade Adjusted Pace takes into account the steepness of terrain during your runs and estimates an equivalent pace on flat land. Because running uphill requires extra work, your Grade Adjusted Pace on ascents will be faster than your actual pace. Similarly, when running downhill, your Grade Adjusted Pace will tend to be slower than your actual pace.

The difference between GAP and actual pace generally becomes larger as the grade steepens. Athlete data has shown that the downhill adjustment peaks around -10%, after which it becomes slightly less extreme. Note that GAP does not account for the technical difficulty or condition of the terrain.

I don't have the book handy to confirm, but I believe that in Training Essentials for Ultrarunning, Jason Koop recommends Strava's GAP as one way to monitor training over variable terrain.

Law 12 doesn't define a fixed threshold. The referee has to decide whether the player was attempting to deceive the referee. The cautionable offence is:

attempts to deceive the referee, e.g. by feigning injury or pretending to have been fouled (simulation)

The amount of contact isn't the deciding factor. What matters is whether the referee believes the player is reacting to the challenge or trying to influence the decision. A player who dramatically exaggerates minor contact to sell a foul for a harsher sanction may also be guilty of attempting to deceive the referee. And of course the viewpoint of the referee matters. Just because we see it, doesn't mean the referee does.

That's why the threshold is usually much higher. A mistaken caution for simulation is difficult to undo, while simply waving play on rarely causes controversy. Unless the deception is obvious, many referees keep the card in their pocket. That's why Law 12 arguably allows more cautions for simulation than are actually shown... especially to players who are well known for their exaggeration.

The simple answer is that however unlikely that is to be, two teams could theoretically end up with the exact same rating, down to two decimals places. You don't want to have to figure out a tie-breaker on the fly for what is arguably one of the most watched sports event on the world.

More realistically, I would hazard that this is at least initially surely a left-over from when FIFA first switched to the current ranking system in 2018. Ratings were initially rounded to the nearest integer; which could readily result in two teams having the exact same rating at a given point in time. This happens for ex. all the time in chess (where there are arguably many more rated competitors, but even looking at say the extreme end of the distribution, the top 100, will reveal several ties: see the FIDE rating list on their website). Looking at the current FIFA ratings (as of July 11th 2026) also reveals a few teams which would in effect be tied if the numbers were rounded to the nearest integer; in fact even some teams which are separated by only 0.01 rating points:

FIFA changed the rounding to two decimal places in April 2021, thereby greatly reducing the potential for ties of this kind, but not eliminating it. The first ratings published after this change in fact even included two pairs of teams tied with the same rating(!), see here. Unless the mentioned teams don't play any games, or only play draws against each other (resulting in no exchange of points), the mathematical coincidences required for this to persist over several rating periods are however vanishingly unlikely.

So, TLDR, it might be unlikely but it's not impossible.

The whistle is NOT needed to:

and

If the referee wants the player(s) to wait for the whistle before restarting play (e.g. when ensuring that defending players are 9.15m (10 yd) from the ball at a free kick) the referee must clearly inform the attacking player(s) to wait for the whistle.

A referee's decisions are final, so unless you can show a misapplication of the LoTG, corruption, or some other serious integrity issue, the result stands. They are not immutable, but they are very hard to get overturned.

Law 5

The decisions of the referee regarding facts connected with play, including whether or not a goal is scored and the result of the match, are final.

If the referee says they judged a situation as violent conduct, serious foul play, abusive language, whatever, the match result normally survives that. A bad factual decision is usually just that... bad, but final. The competition might later cancel a red card suspension, or punish the referee, but the result usually stays.

A wrong application of the LoTG is different. If the referee gets the rules themselves wrong, then the competition rules may allow a protest. For example, calling a penalty for a foul on the halfway line. But this depends on the competition's rules.

And if the issue is not just incompetence but actual bias, corruption, match-fixing, or deliberate manipulation, then it becomes a disciplinary matter. The referee could be suspended or banned, and the league authority may have powers to order a replay (depending on the competition rules).

So for your example of penalties and cards galore: whether the result is overturned would depend on whether this was merely terrible refereeing, a misapplication of the Laws, or something like proven corruption.

Looking at the rules I come upon an interesting property. Each group winner playing against a third place finisher has five possible groups to pick their opponent from.

There is a total of twelve groups, from which eight will see their third place team through, i.e. and conversely four groups will not. This means that there is a good chance that one group winner will have only one possibility left. In addition, even if the former statement is not true, if the third-placed team of group L is through, they can only play against the winner of K (as that is the only combination where they are listed) [15th row in the table, M87]; and the reverse is also true, the third-placed team of K can only play against the winner of L [8th row in the table, M80].

There is no specific mention of equipment interferring with play other than fielding helmets in the Laws of cricket (28.3).

This would thus be a situation for the umpires to adjudicate if it were to happen. Unintentional interference is not generally punished (the law for obstructing the field even specifically excluding accidental incidents from consideration, 37.2); and in the circumstances you describe, it would in fact not seem like the bottle caused much interference if the runner is out by a significant margin. This would not be much different from the ball deflecting unexpectedly off of an uneven patch on the ground.

Placing a water bottle on the field is however very much intentional, and considering that the Laws make provisions for drinks intervals, it could well be argued the same penalty as for helmets should be applied, even if the interference on play is generally going to be of a lesser magnitude than if the ball were to hit a helmet. I'd probably favour this interpretation as well; there's simply nothing in the Laws as written which makes it clear that this is the case.

Yes if you are an elite athlete; around 2008-9 there was a huge "technology war" in swimming which ended up with all elite athletes wearing full-body polyurethane suits due to the performance advantages they give. Most world records were broken in this time, often by considerable margins.

Restrictions have been introduced since then which mean that knee-length jammers are the maximum coverage allowed for men, and similarly knee-length suits which don't cover the shoulders or arms for women. These probably still give a performance advantage over traditional swimwear, but less so.

Whether jammers give your average recreational swimmer a performance advantage is a different question, but the "I want to look like the pros" effect is real and significant.

The holes in a pickleball affect how air moves around (and through) the ball as it spins, which changes how the ball moves through the air. The size and number of those holes definitely has an impact, and the irregular position of the holes in a wiffle ball makes the movement more unpredictable (or predictable if you know how to align them).

Baseballs and golf balls have similar effects from the seams and dimples, but the effects are different by design. Golf balls have dimples to reduce drag, while the seams on a baseball create uneven air movement which changes the ball flight as it spins.

Wiffle ball holes are also horizontal, much longer than the holes of a pickleball. How does that affect the way it flies compared to a pickleball?

It changes the effect of those holes on the flight - spinning the ball in the direction of the "slots" has a different effect than spinning it perpendicular to the slots. This is one way wiffle ball pitchers can control the movement to some degree.

The very first fields were very much improvised (this early game is taking place on what looks very much like a cricket pitch), nor does it appear in any previous rulebook. This is common -- at all levels, high school, college, and NFL -- on punts. After the ball is punted, a few different things can commonly occur:

  • a player from the receiving team catches the ball (either "on the fly" or after a bounce) and attempts to advance. Players from the kicking team try to tackle the receiver.
  • a player from the receiving team makes a "fair catch" -- they catch the ball on the fly and make no attempt to advance. The play is dead at that point and the kicking team are not allowed to make contact with the receiver
  • no player from the receiving team tries to possess the ball. This is likely what you have seen: The ball will be "downed" at the point a member of the kicking team first touches the ball or if no one does, wherever the ball comes to rest*. Until the ball is downed or at complete rest, it would be legal for a receiving team member to grab the ball and attempt to advance, so it is common for members of the kicking team to surround the ball, especially if it is slowly rolling backwards (from the receiving team perspective). The kicking team is gaining a (slight) advantage in yardage and by surrounding the ball, making it highly unlikely that a receiving team member will risk trying to get the ball.

My (admittedly anecdotal) experience is that at the high school level it is much more common for no receiving member to attempt to catch the ball, while in the NFL one of the first two outcomes listed above is much more likely.

(*) There are a few details about exactly how and when a ball is "downed" on a kick, but this is the basic idea.

There are a few possibilities I can think of that I would consider in this situation in order to get into a position to play the black - none are particularly easy...

  1. Play the shot with running side (right-hand spin), and maybe a touch of top-spin, aiming the object ball to the far jaw of the pocket; that is, the right-hand side of the pocket. The object of this is to canon the cue ball into the black ball, running it off the bottom rail and off the side rail moving it into a more favourable position and opening up multiple pockets.

  2. Play the shot straight, with screw and a little check-side (left-hand spin). The object here is to screw the cue ball of the side rail, and with the check-side the cue ball will move further up the table, leaving a more manageable angle on the black ball into the same pocket as the striped ball.

  3. Play the shot to hit the object ball into the rail just before the pocket, and play with screw. Because of the pockets on American pool tables being angled (rather than rounded on English pool tables), the pockets are quite forgiving as to the accuracy needed, as such you can hit the object ball into the rail first, and it still goes in. Doing so will open up the angle of the screw giving it a similar effect to number 2 above.

Experience and ability would probably be the main factor in choosing which approach to go for:

  • Option 1 is probably the most difficult as it would require a bit of finesse and touch to judge the amount of spin to apply to get the required canon, and you're relying on a little bit of luck with the canon.
  • Option 2 would require a decent amount of power as well as good cueing - adding side spin with the additional power would push the cue ball off-line, meaning greater sighting/aiming is required.
  • Option 3 is probably the easiest of the three, but still requires good cueing.
Basically, yes. You don't even need to call "combo". As long as the cue ball strikes your group first and the ball you call goes in, you get the next shot.

According to Baseball-Reference, after 6 games in the 2013 season John Buck had a BA of .400 and OBP of .391. I assume that's what's being referred to here

In those 6 games he had 23 plate appearances, of which 8 were hits, 12 were non-productive outs, 1 was a walk, and 2 were sacrifice flies. He had 8 + 12 = 20 total at-bats, so his BA was 8/20 = 0.400. He had (BB + HBP)/(BB + HBP + SF) = (1 + 0)/(1 + 0 + 2) = 1/3 = 0.333. His OBP was therefore 9/23 = 0.391.

When (BB + HBP)/(BB + HBP + SF) < H/AB then you get OBP < BA - in this case we have that, with 1/3 < 8/20. But this is rare, because walks are much more common then sac flies. For example in the 2013 season as a whole there were in MLB 14640 walks, 1536 HBP, and 1219 SF, so (BB + HBP)/(BB + HBP + SF) = 0.930! It will only happen with small samples, early in the season.

In simple English: blocking is when the ball goes from the opponent, I (we) jump and prevent/try to prevent it from entering our side. The ball can miss our hands, it can go through the block to our side, can go "out", it can rebounce to the opponent's arms, or anywhere else - it is still a block. Also I can block with my head (I dream) if it is higher than the net. And the ball can touch many blockers: it is still one collective block.

now:

FIVB rules

from the official FIVB rules 14.1.1, 14.1.2, 14.1.3:

Blocking is the action of players (1) close to the net (2) to intercept (3) the ball coming from the opponent (4) by reaching higher than the top of the net, regardless of the height of the ball contact

A block attempt is the action of blocking (5) without touching the ball.

A block is completed whenever (6) the ball is touched by a blocker.

(1), (2), ..., (6) - are mine

more details

(1) close to the net there is no exact definition of "close to the net" - sometimes it could be 1m, and the "Beach Volleyball Casebook" even says "it can depend of how tall the blocker is", because a taller blocker can jump farther from the net and his arms are still pretty close to the net. So it's the referee's decision, but usually it is obvious.

(2) to intercept - there is another question about "intercept by spiking", I think people will add the oficial ruling for curious cases to that question: sports/q/16103

(3) from the opponent - the ball must come from the opponent, and it is not a block when a player "imitates the block action" after a set.

(4) higher than the top of the net - what is often missed here: a blocker must have something (arm, finger, nose) higher than the top of the net. So, if my pinky is higher than the net - I can save the ball with my foot and it is still a block.

(5) blocking without touching - libero can not even TRY to block (14.6.6). So in a weird case when a back-row player of TeamA attacks from the first line higher than the net (which is forbidden), and a TeamB libero attempts to block (any part of the body higher than the net) - it is libero's fault, because the attacker's error occurs AFTER libero's error (attack is completed when the ball completely crosses the net/is touched by an opponent -- FIVB 13.1.3). Weird case, but obviously: the action can be a block, even without a contact with the ball.

(6) the ball is touched by a blocker - this definition allows back-row player to "attempt to block", and if the ball didn't touch ANY blocker ("ANY" is important) - then the block is not "completed", and thus - legal.

Also, one can "block the block" - if the ball rebounced from opponent's block and the player is intercepting it back - then it is a "block of another block"

This part acts as a great tie-breaker.

The infield fly rule essentially only removes the risk of a force out of the runners originally on 1st and 2nd. Once the call is made, the batter is out, so that the other runners are not required to move to the next base. However, the ball is still a fly ball, and if caught, the runners must tag before they can safely advance to the next base.

If the ball is caught, the baserunners can attempt to advance as they would on a typical ball caught in the air. MLB Infield Fly Rule
